title: Is one hundred and sixty eight divisible by twelve?
description: The row of primes of twelve is found inside the row of primes of one hundred and sixty eight, and the leftover primes make the other factor. Keeko doubts this and says an extra seven means it is not divisible.
teaching_notes: One idea: extra primes in the number are fine, as they form the other factor. Watch for students who think the divisor must have exactly the same primes.

source: Is 168 divisible by 12? Find the prime factorisations of bot
video_script.why: The child sees that a number is divisible when the primes of the divisor are all present, and the leftover primes make the other factor.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers, one hundred and sixty eight and twelve
video_script.anchor: the rows of primes of one hundred and sixty eight and twelve, with the row of twelve ringed in the front of the longer row
video_script.wrong_answer: an extra seven means it is not divisible
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees a seven in the row of one hundred and sixty eight that twelve does not have, and thinks it blocks divisibility.
video_script.payoff_line: One hundred and sixty eight is twelve times fourteen

final_answer.spoken: one hundred and sixty eight is twelve times fourteen

maths_rules: multiplication can be done in any order: 168 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 × 7
the leftover 7 goes into the second group 2 × 7 and does not block divisibility
video_script.design: The row of one hundred and sixty eight is regrouped so that the primes of twelve stand at the front. The leftover primes form the second group.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about one hundred and sixty eight and twelve.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>One hundred and sixty eight is two times two times two times three times seven. Twelve is two times two times three.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is one hundred and sixty eight divisible by twelve?

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>A number is divisible by another when the primes of the other are all included in its primes.
<bookmark mark='order'/>We may also multiply the primes in any order.

beats.on_screen: To find: whether the row of 12 sits inside the row of 168
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find whether the row of twelve sits inside the other row.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: the row of 168 has the primes 2, 2 and 3 of the row of 12, and also one more 2 and a 7

marks.look: 2, 2 and 3 in the row of 168 light up and match the row of 12

narration: <bookmark mark='look'/>Step one, look for the primes of twelve in the row of one hundred and sixty eight. Two, two and three are all there.

narration: <bookmark mark='move'/>Step two, we can multiply in any order. Move the three forward, so two, two and three stand together at the front.

narration: <bookmark mark='front'/>Step three, make a number from each group. The front group is twelve.
<bookmark mark='back'/>The group left behind is two times seven, which is fourteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: the front group is exactly the row of 12, and the group behind is a whole number

beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes, 168 = 12 × 14, so 168 is divisible by 12

marks.ans: the answer is boxed in green

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes. One hundred and sixty eight is twelve times fourteen, which means it is divisible by twelve.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

<bookmark mark='seven'/>But the seven is no problem, because it goes into the second group.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>What matters is that all the primes of twelve are there.
